Magdalene, and to the Church of James the Brother of the Lord. The strannik pointed out all those places, and al w:iys toil wiier.'iT WWI IleCE,,ftry to contribute money. They returned for dinner to the hostelry ; and after linner,,jo4 as they were getting ready to go to bed, the st rannik began to say Akh, to shake his el Whes, to search. " I have been robbed," he says," of my portnionet, with my money. Twenty- three rubles," says lie, "there we. in it—two ten. rattle notes, and ;direr in change." The stninnik mourned, mourned ; nothing to be done ; they lay down to

Yellin lay down to sleep, and temptation fell upon him. "The strannik's money was not stolen," he thinks "he didn't have any. Ile never gave any. Ile toll me where to give, but he himself did I not giver yes. and he borrowed a ruble of me." Thus Yetim thinks, and then he begins to scold himself. Why," says lie, "In I judge the man? Ido wrong. I won't think about it." As It,' becomes sleepy, again begins to think how sharp the strannik was about money, anti bow he tells an unlikely story aliout his portainnet being stolen. " Ile hadn't any money," he thinks. " WMIA a trick."

Next morning they got up, and went to early mails in the great Church of the Resurrection; to the tomb of the Lord. The strainnik does not leave Yellin : he goes with him everywhere. They Went to tile chnrch. A great crowd of people weiv collected togs her, of pilgrim-rt riinniks, Itti,,rians,anol all peoplos - of Greeks and Armenians, and Turks and Syrians. Yefim entered the sacred gates with the people. A monk led them. Ile led them past Turkish guards to the place where the Saviour was taken from the cross, and anointed, ntnni where the nine great candlesticks aro burning. 1110 points :out every thing. and tells them every thing. Here Yefim placed a Then some monks led Yefim to the right hand nip tint, little flight of steps to Golgotha, where the cross stood. Here Yefim said a prayer. Then they pointed out to Yetim the hole where the earth had opened down to hell ; then they pointed out the place where they had fastened Christ's bands mid feet to the cross ; then they showed the tomb of Adam, over whose hones Christ's blood had flowed ; then they came to the stone whereon Christ had set when they put on him the crown ot thorns ; then thrive pillar to which they hound Christ wlem tlt•y scourged him ; then Ye UM saw like stone with two hollows for Christ's feet. They wore going to show them something more, lint the crowd were in a innirryn they all rushed to the very grotto of the LOrlre sepulchre. There the foreign mans had just ended, the orthodox mass was just beginning. Yellin went into the grotto with the throng. Ile was anxious to get rid of the striinnik, for continually in his thoughts he was sinning against the strannik but the striinnik would not too got rid of; in company with him he goes to Mass at the Lord's sepulchre. They tried to get n,'nrorn they did not get there in time. The people are wedged no clove that them Ia no going forward or hack. Yefim stands, gazes forward, says his prayers; but it is no use ; he keeps feeling whether his purse is still there. Ile is divvied in his thoughts ; one way lie thinks the strannik is deceiving him; the other, he thinks, "fir, if he is not deceiving me, and lie was really robbed, why, then, it might be the Same with me also."

There is also to be an improved trick to lift barg.s from the Weaver into the Weston . Canal and bark again. In the days to come Weston roint is going to be an important Cheshire port. Just now it is only half awake, andthe careworn and taciturn , bargee pervades it. How- I•ver, all is going on briskly, and after seeing what Mr. IValker's people eon do under water an well Os upon dry land, I feel convinced that, with time and money, as, • old Brunel used to say, he would have no hesitation in prolonging the Ship Canal acryss St. tioorge's Channel if Ile were regained to do it.

All the same, Icon pity the unfortunates whose lot ! is cas in less delight fat places, and I can pity the poor fellows who flee from the van that to coming, for I have been there myself. Apart from the "alleged "—convenient wor I that, it keeps you out :of no end of libel cases apart from the " alleged " nuisances at the Intercepting be pots, of which I have not much personal know- ledge, I eon, &Oil 110 Without hesitation endorse the generally expressed opinion of that portion of the public whose nasal organs are in working order that the perambulating vans of" essences that infest our streets are in all respects most I evil things. It is no use saying they don't smell ; they do to most abominably, and everybody known it. Why, I have seen the very tails in the !street hang their dogs, or the very dogs in the street . hang their tails, to put it correctly, on the approach ,of one of these disease-dealing nuisances. This is rather a strong way of speaking, it may be thought, , but is it not the truth ? Is it not a fact that where noxious odours like tress are I here is also disease - planting here and there its fatal germs amongst the ranks of an unoffending pnblie. It is not only plain speaking that is naptiredolear boys, but plain acting, and if you wont to know " Wheer you should be workint now," I tell you plainly that you ought to be working to send men to tine Council Chaniber Will PP that the nuisance is removed, or the vans, and the Dep4ts too, swept off the face of the earth to make room for some system or other that can be carried ottt without affecting the comfort and health of the ratepayers. I have no system to suggest. perhaps you have not ; all that we want it that the present nuisance should be for ever annihilated,and if .11derman Burgess can prove that mom money I still would have that much desired effeet he can have it and weleonie. But he and his Committee must give some proof oilhat, for the ratepayers an. getting tired of ~eeitig thousands trotting aft, tine other t honsands while the stink remains ever with us. Therefore, brethren, what I have to .3, unto you is this -pull yourselves together and elect representatives who will search this matter to Its very depths, and insist 011 some means being taken to free us from the evils that now afflict at, could say some more, but the subject is oppressive, ' and I would fain have done. In front of where tho lock entrances are to he, there is of isaffse still a conaiderable slice of territory left in to keep out the water until tlw canal shall be completed and pronounced well and truly cut and built from end to end. Immediately behind this natural dam bgtoin has been readied along quite half a mile of the cutting (hereabouts (00 fed breast), the internal facing opera- tions an, going merrily Oh, and the workmen now climb to and from their wooden homes on either bank by long thread-likeladders fixed against the ShIPA. The steam navvies, having Whiffed their mission herealsags, have gone farther up the works, and where we last saw them at work there now rises a series of tall, thin, complicated scaffoldings in the middle of the Ind, suggesting that Mr. Walker is :shout to indulge his workmen with au elaborate firework display. Inquiry of a communicative ganger, however, reveals that haw are the soldiers " or framws within Whith the massive concrete walls of the five Eastham Locks are to be eonstructed—the great gateway which will form the last link between Man- chester and the sea. At low tide over thirty feet of water will be kept in these locks, the sills of which will be eleven feet below the deepest dock rill in Liverpool or Birkenhead. At high lisle the gates will be kept open, to that the canal still have the benefit of the incoming water for a stretch of about twenty Mile& as far as the next locks at Latchford, an arrangement of which the twenty-two acres of docks at Warrington will have the benefit.

div.p: HOW THENAVVIrt UV!,

By Pool Hall Bay we cross a dam that has been pur- posely left in whiM the river wall is rising, and find our- selves ins navvy village, built sheer on the hank of the estuary, shaded 'by the thick foliage of a clump of old trees. Here poultry-raising seems to he the stable Indus- , try of thy female population. We find rest and a supply 1 of ginger ale at a singlimmen's lodging-house of three room, all on the ground floor, of which by grace of the , buxom lady in charge, we make inspection, The tens,- ' men is divided into a sleeping apartment for herself and 1 husband—himself one of a "batty-gang" of piece- workers—a kitchen fitted with an immense cooking- ; range and a fall-deed dining-table, and a large room in 1 which are five double beds devoted to the slumbers of ; ten bachelor navigators. All is mrupulously clean, the bedrooms being fitted with kamptulicon,and the kitchen- 1 refectory neatly sanded. Our hostess, being Imes- tioned, given the. following particulars of the navvy's , life—" My lads," says the motherly woman, "coo earn 1 an avenge of a pound a week each. A rather rough lot, ; sir, but not such brutes stones people would try to ' make out. For instance, they am very cleanly in their habits. Whether at meal times or knocking oft there is a fine for any man who do.n't wash himself before he sits down. That is a rule amongst themselves." IM they live well? Well, the Englishmen do live well, rather. It'seggs and ham for breakfast—l often use fifteen doren of eggs in a week. At dinner-time they will have a twelve pound joint amongst them 'ern, and I've nearly always a cold ham in cut. For tea-supper, 1 usually one meal, lends sausages, or what-not. Living in company,, share and share alike, they can do the thing comfortably, you see; anti I turn a bit for my-1 self out of cooking for them and seeing to them generally. I bake all my bread in an oven under the brow yonder. The Irishmen are per feeders, bacon and scraps of all kinds—sometimes what an Englishman wouldn't give Isia dog. I don't care for the Irish much. I'm told a good many of them send money over to their friends in Ireland to help them jay their rent with ; but I can't say as to that. There are no strong drinks here, or anywhere rn the works. If they want a spree, it's over to Liverpool or up to Ellesmere Port they have to go. Mine are a VP ry steady lot, though, and muele given to reading, draught-playing or dominoes. I can't say they are religious ; rather otherwise; but they work hard for 41s1. an hour—mealy 56 hours a week—and they pay their way. No; they don't save much ; but whose fault is that? A poor navvy thinks himself lucky to work hard and live. You can't call them eXtraVa.gant in eating, either, with this bracing air and the hard labeur. They vest have it, you aim." " What will they do when the canal is made ?" I ask, rather stupidly, as the good woman seems to think. "Do ?" she says, opening her eymu to the fullest extent, "what did they do before it began? and work somewhere else. I suppose. Bless you, there's not a more indepen- dent set of men breathing. If a navvy gets tired of his ; job here, right in the middle sten day's work, as like as not he'll pitch away his pick orshovel and go bra tramp across country, and we nevt.r us. him again. If you've got Money, Spend it, they say ; and miles it's gone, go to mat midget some m:•ro:. Saving for a rainy day's non- sense, Owl' think, when all their days are rainy alike. They're taught to work heel for ahoy' aubeistence, and look forward to dying in the h.pital or a workhouse, as all their friends and relations have done before them. You must give a man isimething to save before you begin to Imture him on putting by. As it is, hand to inouth's the rule, and it eaves a lot o trouble, digit you think ?"

div.head: BEAUTIFUL SNOW.
div.p: BEAUTIFUL SNOW.

The author end subject of the following poem was an American actress, who formerly lived in great style and magnificence--a woman of great genius and beauty, fallen from her proud estate. Oh: the snow, the beautiful snow, Filling the sky and earth below ; Over the housetops, over the street, Over the heads ot the people you meet, Dancing, flirting, skimming along. Oh' the snow, the beautiful snow. How the flakes gather, and laugh as they go Whirling about in the maddening fun. ilt plays n its glee with every one. Chasing, laughing, hurrying, by, It lights on the fam and it sparkles the eye ! And the dogs with a birk and a bound. Snap at the crystals that eddy hround ; The town is alive and im heart as glow, To welcome the coming of beautiful snow! How wildly the crowd goes swaying alnng. Hailing ea, bother with humour and wing ! How the gay sledges, like meteors, flash by, Bright for tile moment, then lost to the eye. Hinging, swinging, dashing they go. Over the crust of the beautiful snow Snow so pure when it bills from the she, To be trampled in mud by the vets.' molting by : To he trampled and tracked by the thousands of feet Till it blends with the filth in Dm horrible street. Once I was pore as the snow—but I fell! Fell like the snowiflakes from heaven to hell ; ND to he trampled as filth of the street ; Fell to be stilted, to be spit on, and brat. Pleading, cursing, dreading to die' Sidling my soul to whoever would buy, Dealing in shone fora morsel of bread. Hating the living and fearing the des Merciful tind ! have I fallen so low And yet, I was once like (he beautiful snow. Once I vras fair as the beautiful snow, With an eye like im crystal, a lama like its glow! Once I was loved for my innocent grace— Flattered and sought for the charm of Illy face' Father, mother, sisters Doh and myself, I have lest by iny fail Tle• veriest wretch that goes shivering by. Will make a wide sweep lest I wander tio nigh ; For all Duit is on or above toe, I know, There is nothing, that s pure as the beautiful AnOW. How strange it should be that this beautiful snow Should fall otto sinner with nowhere togs ! Now strange it should be, when the night comes again, If the snow and the ice struck my desperate brain. Fainting, freezing, dying alone, T wicked for prayer, too weak for a moan TO be heard in the streets of the crazy town, thine mad in the joy of the snow coming down, To be, and so die in my terrible woe, With a bed and a shroud of the beautiful snow.

div.head: " WIIEER ARE WE WORKIN' NOW." OTHERWISE KICKS FROM KO-KO."
div.p: " WIIEER ARE WE WORKIN' NOW." OTHERWISE KICKS FROM KO-KO."
[BY i

" Wheer are we workin' now," seems rather a funny title for a newspaper article, doesn't it? But no matter. I apologise to Mr. it erid;n,n for using it in this conneetion, but it seems to ni.• to be ap- propriate. If we are not working now, we should be, and that's a fact. By "we" I do not mean the editorial system that controls this journal, but tine great public of Warrington—the public that should be powerful, and isn't ; the public that should kick, and doesn't ; the public that always talks and seldom acts, and Inns come to be known as the ("rem Ass.- In a town like this the rate-paying inhabitants should Inc able to do pretty muck as they lik,' but they don't seem to know it. They grumble and pay, and by way on a change they pay .d grumble, but the big bugs get there every time all the same. This public wants rousing up; it wants prodding. If it does get roused there will be a shindy. If it can only be induced to kick somewhat, there may be good times coming in more ways than one. It o all very well to ask" Wheer are we workin' now." and then laugh, but the question is where ought we to be working, and in what din;ction, and if you'll allow me I'll soon tell you. " Christmas comes but once a year," and the same applies to

'Tills MUNICIPAL -tiLECTIONS. At Christmas we all celebrate, and make a big thing of it, and when it is past it is forgotten. When the elections Conte On we dOtet Celehnee, we don't make , a big thing of it, and we don't think very much about it either. flow is this? Simply because the " Great A." thinks more about the present than the future. It eats, and drinks, and makes merry-- when the funds run to it—and pays no heed to the things that are to corn.'. With all respect to those whom I am now a loressing, I submit that this is not exactly as it should be. Hence the eccentric title that heads this lucubration. If sae are not working now, we should be. and we should be work- ing to put men in the Council who won't be like dumb clogs" -I beg pardon, some of those now in the Council are anything but " dumb," but for the matter of that it moult perhaps be as well if they Were—What I mean to say is that we should put men on the governing body who will represent us, and not themselves, and who will not be cajoled into "swimming with the stream so much as a lot of them seem to do. As I one year follows another, we allow the political wire-pullers to settle what to as are very import- ant affairs, and we never seem to dream of kicking. No, we simplv pay, and grumble, and play the Juggins, when we ought to rule the roast. We are like a baby beginning to walk--we have the strength but are very much afraid of using it. Let us throw off our swaddling clothes; put away childish things ; and play the man. If the party men put up candidates of whom we approve, send them in. If we don't approve, we must put up candidates of our Own and send them in. Above an, let us avoid political considerations in a local matter like this. On Monday evening a meting to further consider the proposal to erect a suitable memorial to the late Mr. William Delmont WU held at the Town Hall, , under the presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), who had requisitioned it. At a previous meeting held with the same object in view, there • was only a small attendance, and it was then decided that another meeting should be held, on an evening, 80 as lo give the general public an opportunity of ' being present. The attendance on Monday evening, however, was disappointing to those gentlemen who I take an interest in the matter, as there were only fourteen persons present, including two who , occupied seats in the portion of the Council Chamber , net apart her the accommodation of the public, who I did not take any part in the pea endings. div.p: THE GREAT GAL.
GALLANT LIFEBOAT WORK.

A furiims gale sprang up in tine early hours on hlinnilav morning, and although during the day it moderated somewhat, the weather was very boisterous up to a late hour at night. In Liverpool many whams were blea-n down and injured, and slates and ehhnnev-cans were dis- lodged from the houses, while In the sulimilw trees and in some instances walls were blown down. A heavy sea prevailed not only outside the bar but in the Mersey itself, in which the ferry traffic was carried on with groat difficulty. The Liverpool lifeboat was twice 1/I.:t - • once in attempting to aid the crew of a distresscil vessel, which was meanwhile towed into the river, :and once under similar circumstances on the information I that a large timber laden vessel, thehtount Pleasant, was ashore off lloylake. The crew were conveyed to the Sailors Home. Fronnali parts on tin, country come reports of damage and disaster. It is reported that at Holyhead two big gaps have been made in the breakwater, the damage being estimated at £20,000. About eight o'clock in 'the morning tine tog London gave information at the hew Brighton stage that a small vessel had been seen in the Crosby Channel making signals of distress. The crew at eget mustered, and is a few minutes left the stage in tow of the tug tiladiator, but when off Crosby sine shipped a tremendous sea, which broke the hawier and filled the lifeboat. After about three-quarters id mahout's VAlrk the crew bated out the boat, and getting another hawser attached. proceeded to the Crosby Lightship. They could not get near enough to hail the crew iif the Lightship, but tin latter signalled that the venael in distrnmhad been towed , into port by n passing tug. The lii.bnat, therefore, , went, bark to NeNi Brighton under mil. . .

DetaiFs-are to hand of the wreck off tie Isle of Man of t the Norwegian ship St. George, which left Greenock or. Sattuday rimming with a gent.ral cargo for Monte with a crew .4 22 hands and the captain's wife and • babe nine months old. During the •gale on Sunday night off the west coast of the Isle of Man the forematit and rigging went, and the newel became unmanageable. She lay for twelve hOUTO in this plight, aml was passed • by a steamer which refused to lend aid. hhe mom sighted . from Peel on Monday forencmn, and at one o'clock the lifehoat John Monk was launtimi, and proceeded in the teeth of a north-westerly gale to the drifting ship, which , was three or four miles bff land. It was tbought impos- sible for the lifeboat to get to her, but aft, two hours' ' splendid sailing, such as Ims neon been seton on the Mann I I coast before, the lifeboat got up. Not being able to get ' alongside of the wreck, the crew of twen.y-two were , hauled from the ship into thelifehoat by moans of a life- hoop at the end of a hawser. 'The captain o wife was I brought first, then the carpenter with the le.bv sewed in eanvas and lashed to his shoulder, the captain being laet. [Within an hour of the hooting of the crew the vessel , drifted on to the rocks near lOvl With. and 'sum totally I wrecked.

Telegraph communication was restored on Tuesday, MA the weather continued rough. On Wetimisday SOCM parts of the country there War a partial renewal of the gale. At ttlaeltpiwil a violent north-easterly wind raked a tempestuous sea, and the waves washed over the proinenade bra considerable portion of its length. At Ssndgate and Ilythe the sea wall custained consider- able ilainag,e. News has reached Liverpool of the safety lof the Arklow, which left tie, Mersey n Saturday, and was suppers] to have been wrecked en the neighbour- hood tif Aberystwitb.

T:te Cabinet Portrait Gallery" is the title of a new venture by Messrs. Cassell St Co. Judging I from the first part, it is likely to be highly appre- ciated, and, therefore, successful. The portraits are photographs by Messrs. W. St D. Downie, and it is ! needless to ray that, coming from so eminent a , time, they are artistically and highly-finished speci- i wens of work. They are mounted on card-board, and are, therefore, if it were thought tit, ready for framing. There are three portraits in the first num- her, the find being of the Duke and Duchesa of Fife, the second of Sarah Bernhanit, and the third of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Accompanying , each portrait, there is a brief memoir of the tele- brines photographed. " The Days of the Year" is a poetic calendar front the works of Alfred Austin, “selected and edited by A. 5.," and published by Mr. Walter Scott, London. The select- ing has been carefully done, and the quotations—one for every day in the year—are, for the most part, exceed- ingly appropriate. Mr. Alfred Austin does not reach the highest rank as a poet, but he may be classed as one of the first of the minor poets, and it is due to hint to say that his phrasing has often something of Shakespear- ian stmngth in it. 'Take for instance such a couplet as— •• Amazonian march with torean half lore,' . .

Ale:l7;et;. ' q;s:ing' Tt.he7l;:. There is an introductory note fnan the pen of Mr. W. . Sharp, who, as might be expected, is discrimipating as ' well as sympathetic. The volume is one Ail, return to be highly poised by all lovers of verse and healthy senti- ment.

Erum the same firm we have in theNovocastrian series I of shilling novels an Australian romance, entitled "Tine Kara Yerta Tragedy." It is from the pen of Mr. J. E. Harrison, and it is altogether an interesting story. The plot of the tragedy is admirably worked out, tacit detail being made to work into the main incident. There is just a little stretch of probability here and there, but that is what we suppose is to be expected in a novel of this character. The descriptions of Australian life and scenery certainly help to give special character and interest to the story. •"fhe Life of Sheridan," by Mm. Oliphant, reaches no ;in the English Men of Letters, published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. This story cf the career of a brilliant writer and statesman is brilliantly told. The interest never flags, and the facts are set forth to as to do justice to the strength no well as to the weakness of Sheridan's character. We get to see the was as be is, and for those who require It there is innch aihnirable criticism of his methisis and work, and of the characters It,' has delineated in his wonderful comedies. Messrs. Macmillan have made a bold venture in announcing the publication of Charles Kingsley's novels month by month at the small stun of sixpence each. I The first to hand is for Oetolar, and the story iralled " Westward 110." Nothing better could be put in the hands of the yonang, or for that matter, of the old, tor whilst the incidents are exciting they are soundly based upon the history of our country, and the sentiment throughout is bresay and wholesome. It should be added that the sixpenny volume is one of 1.50 large and closely but well•printol lager. We cannot doubt but the under- ; taking will be a great success.

This was no well received, that Dr. Hyde j has been induced to largely extend it, and, by giving a J great amnia of additional information, he inakes the ; ; work of permanent ate for reference purposes. The East-end is seeking now to improve the ! condition of half-starved female toilers. At a ' meeting, presided over, on Tuesday. IT the Bishop , of Bedford, it was resolved to form a Trades Union, and establish a WOlllell'S Labour Bureau. It will ' be difficult, undoubtedly, to organise women workers: hut the greater the difficulty the greater the triumph, if a triumph In, achieved. lu many . cases, women in London are work for less than one penny per hour. THE tide is still flowing in favour jj'etrir'e%l of the Liberal party. The conn-

try is getting month by month more and more dissatisfied with a Government that has no answer but Coercion to the just demands of the Irish people. The victory of Peter- borough, on Monday, was complete; it resulted in the enemy being driven from the field. The seat was held by an upholder of the Government, who hwl a majority, at the last election of 289. To-day it is occupied by a supporter of Mr. GLAIMON6 : with a majority at his back of 251. The difference between being 209 behind and 2.11 ahead marks the progress tef the electors towards the wise and beneficial policy of Home Rule. The Tories see it, awl some of their journals are candid enough to confess that they are being beaten. Others say, as MIMI, that a bye-election is of no con- sequence ? It never is of oonsequence until they happen to will one as at Doncaster, and then they scream themselves hoarse in culling attention to the fact. But those who doubted as to how the tide was flowing, inn Monday, would perhaps be convinced when they heard the result, on Welbeete day, of the Elgin and Nairn election. This :in undoubtedly another Liberal gain, though it is not a Parliamentary gain. The seat was previously held by a Liberal, Mr. C. H. A NIINRSON, who was returned :it the lest election by a majority of 119. If, as the I;teionists boasted, they were making headway in Sesdland there was rO/0011 to hope that they would Inc able to win Elgin and Naini ; and they fought ;es if they meant to win. But they are beaten, and badly beaten. Mr. J. S. Kane the Liberal candidate is returned by a major- ity of 229 -the majority, by a curicnni coincidence, which Mr. McMismas obtained in Warrington in 1000. The 11011 wadi a largo ono ; 2,273 votes for the Liberal, and 2,411 for the Unionists. In 1886, there were many abstentions; the rank and tile were disturbed and confused by the split amongst the leaders of the Liberal party. They have had time to think the Home Rule problem out for themselves, and they have COMO tO Ow conclusion that it is the, only way out of the Irish difficulty. Hence their eariumetnowe, their enthusiasm, the vic- tories; they are winning. Let it be granted that OM r'v two bye-elections may mislead ; a dozen electenlle are not misleading. The French elections have knocked General Ikmlarger into • cocked hat. He is simply nowhere, and the Monarchists, who have used hits la. a tool, find that instead of gaining strength, they have lost it. Thu General's supplies have already stopped; his base of operations has gone, and he has gone too—to Jersey. It is cheaper living in Jersey than in London. Bye-bye, Boulanger.

The minutes If the Gas and Water Committee con- tained the report of the engineer, who stated that the new bed for the Dinsmore process in No. 2 retort house continued to give good results. Two weeks working with the Abram Arley slack gave the following made per ton 11,300 ; illuminating power, 2074 can- dlm ; tar used per ton of coal carbonized, 44 gallons. The alteration of taking the tar into the duct in a gaseous instead of a liquid form simplified both the plant and the working operation, no extra care and attention being now required over the ordinary stoker's duties. There were at present two beds working on the system ; two more would be started this month, and another two in November, making in all 41 mouthpieces on the Dinsmore plan. The mean rainfall for the month had been 3-235 inches. Daring the month there had been delivered 58,876,000 gallons f water and 7,999,000 cabin feet of gas. The illuminating power of the gas was 1827 candles. A letter frion Mr J. H. Turner to. electric light was considered, and it was recommended that no action be: taken by the Board at pretest—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Wright.

The candidates for the forthcoming election have been chosen, and the battle hat begun. Owing to the advent of Mr. J. IL Lee as an independent, the Nonconformistl have had to alter their programme by dropping the name of Mr. Robert Shaw from , their list. As the first three on the halloted list, the following gentlemen have been selected to cham- pion the cause :—Mr. B. Brown, Mr. T. Snape, and Mr. R. 11. Davis. The Catholic candidates are Dean Finegan, Father Clarke, Dr. o•Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell. , and Mr. S. Quinn. It will he observed that the retiring members seek re-election, with the exception ot Mr. P. A singular question arising from the scores in a Rugby ! match arose at St. Helens, on Saturday. The town club met Lancaster and the result of an uninteresting struggle was as follows :—Last-aster, 1-1-2; St. Ifelens, Mal As the tome team had obtained their goal from a itenalty free kick the Lancastrians contended that it should only count two points, and that they had won the match by four points to three. Them was a looking up of rule books and other authorities on the point and the claim of the visitors was found to be a correct one. The 't in and out " form displayed by the St. Helens town club has not given general satisfaction to their supportem.

The Boundary•roadsters, the Recreation, still continue to show some tip-top play. Their latest victims were the Aspull team, to the tune two goals, two tries, and three minors, to a solitary- minor. A record like this maker ine and many others think, that either the Recreation have enormously Unproved or that the Aspuliites have deteriorated to an alarming extent. Perhaps a little of both ; but As to the improvement of the Recs, there cannot be the slightest doubt.

A FATHER WHO WON'T KaltP HIS CHILDREN. I The Warrington magistrates on Saturday dealt with a DIRD named Joseph Chamock, who was charged with having neglected to maintain his three ohildren, who had become dependent on the Union. After hearing the evidence of Mr. Shearer, they sent Charnock to prison for a fortnight, and remarked that it was evident that he made no attempt to support his family. A SERIKEI OF FELONIES. On Thursday, at the Warrington Police Court, a single woman named Sarah Ellen Richardson (18) was charged with having stolen, on three different occasions, three shawls belonging to work-girls at the Castle Rubber Works, Ellesmere-st., where she also was employed. She pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for a month on one of the charges, a conviction being recorded in regard tothe remaining charges. FURIOVE DRIVING AT BRIDGE-FOOT. The Chief Constable of Warrington, Mr. S. Hunt, on Saturday predicted that some day there will be a fearful collision at the corner of Mersey-st. and Bridge-foot. A man named James Barlow was before the Borough Court on a charge of furious driving at. the spot in question, and Mr. Hunt said that as a rule people drove too quickly over the bridge, where there was a good deal of traffic. Barlow was mulcted in the costs, 3s. ad. THREATENING TO KNOCK A WIFE'S HEAD OFF Edward Walsh, Turner-st.. was before the War- rington magistrates, on Wednesday, on a charge of having used threats towards his wife, on the 7th Complai”- '

Inst._ __iplainant said that he came lie.me drunk, and they had an argument, in the course of which he threatened to knock her head oft She fetched Constable Caldwell to the house, and in the presence of the constable Walsh repeated his threat. He was ordered to find a surety for his good behaviour for the next six months. PERSISTENT WIFE NEGLECT. div.head: FOOTBALL. -ASSOCIATION.
div.p: FOOTBALL. -ASSOCIATION.

What has Caine over " poor Earlestown !" That mis- fortunes never come singly has been mad, manifest in her case. Not only has Earlestown to win its first League match, but last week the club was disqualified front taking any further part in this season's County Cup contest for refusing to play an extra half-hour against Park Lane Wanderers, and on Monday last about one hundred yards of the field-boarding was blown down by the gale which passed over the district. Surely it never rains but it pours ! This too, after a beating of eight goals to two by , Blackpool last Saturday! Pity the sorrows of poor F.arles- , town.

The St. Helens Associationists continue on their sue- censful career and on Saturday they won their way into the second round of the competition for the Liverpool and District Senior Cup by beating Bootle Athletic. The winners played a champion" game all through, and i well earned the cheers of their supporters.

The prize consisted of a handsome marble timepiece.

div.p: TUE MINERS' CONFERENCE.

A typort comes from Sydney that a man named George Winch has just untie into a considerable amount of property in a somewhat remarkable manner. He has been following the occupation of a butcher for some lilac, anti it appeaN he recently took the liberty of kiss- ing one of limo enstomers—a grad-looking girl who dealt atfiis shop. She resented the affront, and had Winch Kt:twitted for assault. He was fined heavily by the local magistrates, and the case attracted much attention from the press. The imblicity given to the pmceedings happened to arrest the notice of a firm of solicitors in Sydney, who had been appointed truatees of certain property which had been left to Winch by a distan relative vane nineteen years ago, and the solicitors were unable to find nay trace of the heir. Winch was com- municated with by the firm, and he has now furnished the history of his antecedents, and .tablished his identity beyond a doubt .

Sir.,:Wrll;iti kindly allow toe, through the cottons of your spiritist journal, to faintly express the pleasure I felt this morning, when I saw in black anti white that there was an impudent little David in liuttermarket-st.. bilking about slinging his little pebble at the head cf the Great Goliath—John Barleycorn, on Saturday nights. I see that the people at Buttennarket-st. school, intend to commence a counter attraction to the publichouse by providing iispolar odertainments, on Saturday nights. The committee invite all who ran, and are interested in such work, to put their shoulders the wheel, and help the Chariot along. I say Ood-speed. The grumlders have had a good long day, and the shirkers have been equally busy. It is high time the workers entered the field. For one. time it has been lelt that some such movement was greatly needed in our good old town. I am convinced that Oils isa step in the right direction, and will supple a long felt want. Man is a social being ;he was made such, and it is as natural for him to sal brightness and congenial com- pany—as it is for the lark warbling to ascend into the blue The bniwers realisot Olis long ago. The children el this ...odd are wiser than the children of light ; hence they know that the money spent in Paint, I ias. and the Fiddle pay infinite per cent. How lamentably slow philanthropists are in these matter.: ! There is a kind of patronising charity that would nmeh rather dole out two and sixpenny worth of soup than give one shilling to prevent such crouching need. How many hundred thousands of pounds are being given annually to bind up the broken heart and broken body, when it is ipate dear to the most cursory observer that one quarter the , amount spent in prevention would do infinitely morn; good. We ask the working-men for their own good, and that el their families. to keep out of tile public-bah.. But where de we ask them to go ? to it wise to ask them to parade the cold, wet, dirty streets ? Is it any use ask- ing them to stay on their own hearthstone? Alas ! how many there are that present no attraction, but the con- trary.. It is no secret that a large percentage of those who become drunkards, after marriage, are driven to the public-houoe through a want of domestic comforts. And, if these are to be saved from the snare something hunt be done—not merely tallest about. What have the Temperance Reformers &ion doing all these years ? A good work certainly, but it iIAS not taken such practical forty as to keep pace with the wily. What are needed are rendervous of brightness and attraction, free from those snares which lead toward the downward grade. Perhaps some will say there are the clubs—Conservative and Liheral.-Can any who have been there say that they are free from the dangers which surround the gin-palace? Alas ! no. I hail with much pleasure the object referred to, anti pray that it may he the commencement of many such. Let all who have a voice, cornet. flute, harp, sarbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and even a tin whistle. respond to the invitation of the Committee and say, Here am I," It is quite certain that there is talent enough to spare in Warrington and neighbourhood to run six such, and make them a thorough success.—Yours respectfully. WILLING TO HELP.

div.head: DIVES AND LAZARUS.
div.p: DIVES AND LAZARUS.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space for one more, and as far as lam concerned, last word on this subject. as Mr. Peers is in the slaying wood, I may as well be killed for a sheep as a lamb. In his first essay his assertion was that the founder of Christianity had consigned Dives to hell because he was rich, and Lazarus to heaven be- cause hi- was a beggar, and that to secure a future in heaven one had only to be idle and improvident. These conclusions I denied, and abler pens than mine have re- futed them entirely. Still he champions Dives, and quotes a partial comment by Dr. Adam Clarke to sub- stantiate his false theory and assertion that Dives was a good man and Lazarus idle, thriftless, and improvident. Mr. Peers quoting the Doctor's words, asks what are his crimes ? First, he was rich ; admitted. Many men are rich, who, if everyone had their own, and the ways and means by which they acquired their wealth were inves- tigated, would be not only poor but criminals. Second, he was clothed in purple and fine linen ; he decorated his body outwardly—a dandy, a swell of the first water. Third, he feasted well, fared sumptuously every day ; no fasts for hull—Lazarus did the fasting. Diem was an epicure, possibly a glutton. Epicurism and gluttony are closely allied. Alr. Peers would have us believe, on the authority of Dr. Adam Clarke, that "he, Dives was blameless "—and, "compared with thousands, vir- tuous " Ile wa.s comparatively virtuous ; that is not saying much. Ile had five brothem,and lie may have been the best in the family. Comparative virtue is a weak quality. Ilis brothers were no great things ; there was something wrong with them—or why should lie with to rend Uterus to warn them ? Virtuous men they were doubtless; blameless men need no warning. Dives' own words furnish the reason for hit being in torment. There was on Ins part unrepented sin, or why would his brothers escape, if they repented Such were his words; if sonic one went to them from the dead they would repent. Ile enjoyed himself to the full when in life—he took his pleasures—and let duty slide. Ile was a sensua- list ; he had his homes, carriages, and dogs—boats, too, very likely. Mr. Peers says I have a wikl untrained imagination ; lam giving it play. I don't thinks man of the Dives , stamp wonkl be without a boat or a ship of some sort. I He could have given to the world through the Press of , his time, wime thrilling narratives of his boating adven- tures—o Mis " hair-breadth 'scapes," of the danger and excitement consequent on his boat " sticking in the,mud." On those occasions it is possible that he may have used some very strong nautical language. Race homeshe must have had. It goes without saying he would patronise the turf. Ile would not be a full blown peer without race horses—for he Was a peer—the progenitor and prototype of peers. I mean nothing personal-1 refer to peers of the blood not the blood Mao blood whirb pm, acquire by virtue of their patents. It would bean intensting study, and Mr. Peers being a man of science, might give us an analysis I of the blood of is peer and the bbeal of a beggar, skew- ing the gradations in the scale upwanls, and that mystic change that take; place in the colour of the blood of a commoner when he is transformed by patent proceed- ings into a peer. Remember I make no charge against rich 'nen collectively. They are much like other men ; some good, some bad. Wealth, when rightly directed, and prudently used, is a blessing. Capital and labour should he ebee friends, and it is a great tnistake that makes them antagonists. With your permission, sir, I will in future revert to tho subject that has been with ine a study for many years—loin to make the poor richer without making the rich poorer. I think the problem may to a great extent be solved without violence or revolution, or anyone tie- ing made the worse, while thousands may be made wrier. Mr. Peers may indulge in blank cartridges, imaginary slaughter, and knuckle rapping to bis heart's content. He may yelp at my bri-ls ; his teeth an- strums; he can- not bite. I heed him not and shall not notice any of the effusions with which he may in future honour your columns. It would be a waste of time to bandy words with a shallow vain man who jumps to unwarrantable esinclusions.-1 am, sir, very respectfully yours, CYMRU. Sankey Bridges, Oct. 7th, 1889.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY:
div.p: THE WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY:

Sir,—Every lover of music must have read with some regret, the report of the annual misting of the Society, published in your columns of Saturday Mat. The report in very unsatisfactory to all concerned, but it is only what any practical person could have expected, for these mmilts were prognosticated months ago, when last the Society and its work were discuss,' in the public ' The President's Statement.—At the time alluded to, I pointed out, that valuable though the mrvices of Dr. Hiles are, they were too valuable for the Society to pay. I I was taken severely to task by nine gentleman, who took up the cudgels on behalf of fir. Hiles. but now Mr. John Dylan& acquiesces in what I then stated, and lie is supported by this same gentleman, no doubt. Mr. Rylands is report,' to have said, that the services of Dr. Hiles were indispensable." If they were indispens- able then, no they are now. thing is indispensable when it cannot. by any imibility, done without . But sew. " reading between the lines, Mr. Itylands infers, . that these services am not indispensable ; that they can be done without ; and why? Because the Society can so longer affordto pay Inc die., What a remarkable •

discovery ! What in genius it must have required to. disrover this, after nearly half a centanT's practical C 1.111,1011 with a musical world ! And how equivocal his position, for 'u thing cannot both be, and not be therc•fore, the Chairman is illogical. Dr. Hiles was not indisporoable to the Society then, nor can he be indis- pensable lathe Society now. Dr. Hilm is a clever man —acknowledged to be no by the best members of his profession—but he is too expensive a conductor for the means of t ho Warrington Musical Society. The Trossurer's litport.—This part of the report explains the weaknms of the business. Dr. Hiles was inid £52 10s., and professional vocalists were paid £68150. id Here are " the 'mike"on which the Society endangers its existence. Of the amount paid to Mr. Pricgor I have nothing to nay; the among Could IN' paid without any inconvenience, if the attain of the Siciety were properly conducted. The valuable services of Mr. Prettier inust be mtainnl. Another item of the report was—, some member; had tickets and did not pay for them nor return them." I quite believe this, aunt very likely it was for these unmannerly swells," tint special trains were engaged, and lint pita ing in an appearance at the concerts, no railway fares were forth- coming, consequently the Society wa.s nalled upon to make gin of the deficiency, to the Land NW. Hallway. Will the Committee allow this to continue ?

...... What N. ma be done ?-1,1 inlkina the following suggem t lint, I an: only repeating what I have before advocated. Fir:4 : The services of Dr. Hiles must be dispensed with, IleMoe •he Society cannot afford to pay for them. A local man must be appointed, and, whoever he may be, he must not be the nominal, Ito clique or particular person ; hot he must be appointool by the members of the Society :del by vote. I once heard an official of the wiety say that, "there was no local man capable if taking the post of conductor." To which I replied " Nonsense." There are no Professional Conductors in the town, but the present ono is not a , s;onal Conductor, that is to say he does not do this exchnively. There are to,, rising young , men and, if either was properly approached. , he would accept the office for a nominal sum. With twelve month.' practice, either would do credit to the Society. They are both popular and well- known to the practical members of the Society ; and any short-comings, at the outset, would be, lam sure, con- siderately treated,both by the band and tire eh a... Snood ; The rehearsals must commence at a reasonable hour, 8 pm. ; for the convenience of members, and pro- bable members, and not for the convenience of any Conductor. This statement is not new ; but it rain uni- son with common sense.—Third : into solo principals ; the Society has been too lavish in this respect ; and wlm is to blame, Secretary or Conductor? I do mot know, but the faehf remains. The Society might, with economy :mead:many engage a •• Star " or two, but to engage expenaive ar istes foreach concert is a mistake. There are artistes " nearer home" than London is: and when concerts and the works to be performed ono feted upon.. the Secretary should at tome place himself in touch with soloists, and give the engagements }dray of ti,or in, advance,. that the former :nay "mock up" the parts • if nee:ma:fry.

Again the Society, as at present conducted, do. not , give young people with good voices and some ability, any envooragement, to work and improve theinselms as soloists. The number of young voices in Warrington capable of taking leading parts, at any concert, may be counted on tin' fingers of one hand. The Soenetyra to blame for this ; lust with the appointment of a local con- ductor, this defect would be remedied, because, being on the spot, he would be able to give occasional private rehearsals to the selected voices. Dr. Hil. cannot be expected to do this. He would have to come from Man- chester apecially, and even if he did set he would require paying for lila labour, and the Society cannot afford it. To train a chorus inane thing ;to train soloists is quite another matter. lam only speaking generally, for the training set vocal soloists is a distinctive part of the musical profession, and to be accomplished requires special training. The Steretary'r Report :—I endorse every word he says. I know it is so fn experience; and this is tics best of schools. Mr. Jenki. says—" It is no use evading the question." What lam driving at is .• that the loss was occasioned in the dress seats." The sum and substance of his remarks are—. If the society is to be a sucee., you must cater for the middle and working classes and leave • the swells,' out of your calculations." I repeat that Mr. Jenkina is correct. A friend of mime once gave a .ncert, on behalf of a charity in the Public Hall. He catensl for the masses, and handed over £l5 to the charity. He thought that he would try another and cater for the aristocracy ;" he improved chorus and band s printed on Monster Poderr a list of the local swells" as patrons—about 30 in number ! Well 25 did not take tickets, but wrote reek sire let:err, k for adver- tising them—on the cheap) ! His only supporters were three vier-presidents of the Musical Society, the same gentlemen who liberally gave last year, to wipe off the debt of the Society. The end of this second concert svas that my friend lust £2. The concert waa on behalf of the Warrington Infirmary. The side galleries and back massacre crowded; the reserved seats were a wilderness. I asked my friend if he would ever give another concert Under Indispeirhed Patrosaye 1” His reply was char- acteriatic but what it was, must remain" in tny pen." —Yours truly,

Sir,—This discussion as to Tolstoi .d his fitness to be a guide in the consideration of what to do to improve the condition of our English poor, bristles with side onerous thickly as ...pills upon the fretful porcupine; " and, were it not that the question demands and ought to have, grave treatment, it would be highly amusing to note how much, in its resultc, it resembles that of a red rag when waved before a bull. And we may measure the estimation in which each of my critics holds the other by the eager haste they display to supplement each other's efforts to overcosne so small an opponent as my- self. Now, my object in writing woo toclear theground before entering into the discussion. As right clean- sions can seldom be arrived at by the adoption of wrong premises, it is better to start fair and with a clear under- standing of the requirements of tha case. . . .

Now,"it is Eng fisl poverty we am considering, until that must be judged by English standards, guided by English experience and observation. What obtains in a purely rural or pastoral country is no guide to the treat- ment of our own poverty, where the condition is so widely different Lot us clear our minds of cant, by which I mean the unthinking repetition of" sing-song " words and ideas. "He who giveth to the poor lencleth to the Lord" will, in these days, not do without qualification. For there are the poor and the pone, the deserving and the undeserving. Now, the deserving poor need and will have front every one deserving the name of man, the most heartfelt sympathy and relief, whenever it can be given. Hut herein comes the difficulty—how are we to distinguish between the two P In II& very artificial state of civilization in which we live, there is such an unhealthy separation between Dives and Lazares that the rich man has no isieans of becoming personally acquainted with the wants and feelings of his less fortu- nate brother. As is only natural, the habits and modes of thought of the well-todo are widely diverse front those of their unleisured and unlettered brethren. And : I think there can te no kind of doubt that this unfortu- nate divergence must act prejudicially upon both. We may hope that the working of the Education Acts may terea, risme eicAsst riejassibring-a- AssiverSerateelaari.i."l taste and feeling amongst "tire lower orders." Tins, ; by assimilating the thoughts and, t. sane extent, the ; habits, of the two, must tend to render intercourse be- tween them easier, and pleasanter than it is at present. A work of lime, this, vou say. Certainly. The evil we I wish to remedy has been of 'slow growth, and the anti- dote eannos be expected to work with the magic celerity of a quack advertisement At preseat I am convinced that our system of society contains either too much or hio little Socialism. Ode forefatheis, appalled by the increase of perennial pauper- I ism, passel the Poor Law At, and there they stopped. Now, this interfered with alum of nature; and all such interferences are had, unless carried out thoroughly and judiciously. This law is far MOP. inflexible and un- avoidable than those of the Med°, and Persians, because aelf-enforcing and self-acting in all rimers of the earth. By the operation of this law, every species on the earth, if it multiplies too fast for the food supply of its neighbourhoexl, must either dicer migrates. find fresh woods and matins new." England being an island makes it bad to migrate from by the totally impecu- nious.

Now the feeling of modern society will nit permit the other alternative to take effect. When aperson, whether from avoidable or unavoidable causes, cannot find the ' means to satisfy his hunger, he falls npon the rates or retires into " the House." Now the Howe is purely a socialiatic institution. Here we have tla. State stepping in and compelling every citizen to contribute,according to his means, towards the mairren.ce of the Hoose and its offfials. And here comes the question, ought not the State to take a step further and compel every man without exerptinn to make some provision against pos- sible if not probable pauperism? As will be wen this is merely an extensii in of the principle of the older Poor's Law. It 1,1 about this that " Cyntro" beCOMPS no hysterically incoherent. At two or thus - points the water effected breaches in the outer em- bankments and flanlesi the cuttings inside. On these embankments rails had been laid for the conveyance of spoil and stone for the outer facing. These rails have been torn up, or undermined, and waggons overthrown. A little further on, where the embankment had not been made, and the tide came in with full force, it reinthed the main line of rails, communicating with the other sections,and for about time yards this was washed out anal thrown out of place, and a considerable space flooded. A little further still a deep cutting of about 100 yards in length is protected by an outer embankment. In this a large breach has !nen made, and the cutting completely flooded, two steam excavators in it standing in about 15 to 20 feet of water. At the tiowy syphon cutting there was a considerable, though not serious, influx of water, which a little extra pumping has overcome. At the eastern extremity of this section, where pile-shriving is in progrem, one of the machines has been overthrown. The important Kanthain action, winch includes an emlankment similar to those deacribed of fully a mile in length. 11.9 fortunately escaped disaster.

HEAVY STORM AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN. A storm of terrible stverity- prevail.' in this neighbourhood on Monday. The wind was blowing ' a hurricane, and rain descended in torrents. At Widnes water lay deep in many roads, and the , cellars of numerous houses and shops were flooded I about the centre of the town. Pedestrians had much difficulty in moving along. Nearly all out- door labour had to be suspended. A large bill-post- ing station near the London and North-Western Railway Station was partially blown down, and numerous chimney lints and slates were ensured in different parts of the town. The road leading to Ditton Junction station WU deeply covered with water and traffic was almost at a standstill in the neiglasiurhood in consequence. In Runcorn the wind played sad havoc with the chimney pas, and slates, but happily no dents are reported. At the railway station a large nulls- her of people had a severe fright. A chimney pot, weighing about 3 cwt, was dislodged from its position, and crashed through the roof on to the boarded ceiling of the general Waiting nom. The ceiling,although split and twisted by the heavy blow, fortunately resisted the massive missile, or serious injuries would have been in. dieted on a number of women and children, who were standing directly underneath. They fled in alarm on hearing the crash. The Mersey receives' the full free,' of the gale, and the water was thrown into foaming waves that sent spray almost as high as Runcorn Bridge. Nevi. galon was rendered not only difficult, but dangerous. No ves.sels ventured out of the docks. Several small beats were dashed to pieces on the beach, And several flats were sunk. A number of hatches from flats were washed ashore on the marsh near Wigg's works. Two barges, belonging to Mr. Walker, Ship Canal contractor, which were lying near Widnes shore laden with rock, were sunk at high water, and the cargo emptied into the river. A crane at the same place was blown down and smashed. On the Runcorn share, the embankment of the Ship Canal railway was attached by the turbulent waters, and sufficient was washed away to render it unsafe to conduct traffic over it. At Randall's sluice, near Norton, the water heat against the massive masonry with great force, and dashing over the tnp flooded the cutting. The masonry sustained damage that it will take weeks to repair. A cutter belonging to the training ship Akbar, of Liver- pool, and manned with 12 boys, drifted up to West. Point, and Captain Clarke, harbour master, seeing its dangerous position, sent the tug Gladiator to the assis- tance of the boys. The cutter was successfully towed into dock. It transpinsl that the boys had been sent to convey the captain's daughter to New For,;, but the fall fury of the ammo broke upon them, and the Wet got beyond their control. The "castaways ' were well cared for until Wednesday morning, when they were towed back to Liverpool.

div.head: ALLEGED DIVE FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE. DID TOMMY DIVE?
div.p: ALLEGED DIVE FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE. DID TOMMY DIVE?

The daily newspapers, on Thursday, gave pro- minence to a description of an extraordinary dive from Runcorn Bridge, into the Mersey, and subse- quent swim as or RA Liverpool, by a man named •• Tommy Burn," The event is described with great circumstantiality. but the strange part of the ban- neon is that no one saw this seeker after fame do the deed, and he must verily have Hashed through the air like a meteor?' A rumour was afloat that Burns intend,' t to di, from the Bridge, on wed- nenday, and s slow look out was kept by the numerous persons employed on the Bridge. Both sides of the lofty structure were watched. Ott the shore, both amine and below the Bridge, the Ship Canal workmen were also on Om watch. Strange to say, neither did they Witneto the dive, nor did they see any person swimming in the river "in fine style' or in any other style. This much woo seen. About two o'clock the pain- ters employed on the high girders saw a man wear- ,lag a long overc tat walk on the Bridge from the ; direction of Widnes, and on reaching half-way he stopped and viewed the "boding flood Ismeath." Ile was then observed to write something on the rail in front of him and to make a note on a piece of paper. lie then retraced his steps and the painters, then curiously excited, descended from their die- voted position in order to ascertain what this mysterious proceeding meant. They found to their amusement the word " Boron" written on the mils; and scratched the marks off with a penknife. This was about two o'clock. A few minutes after that time a man who had gone on the Bridge a quarter of an hour previously again passed through the wicket at the Widnes end of the Bridge, and told the collector that 8111118. dived off the Bridge about 13 minutes since." At the same time begave the collector a carte-de-visit„being his own likeness, i.e., Professor Boston, and the portrait of linms in bathing costume. lie then hurried away as though, says the collector, he wanted to catch a totin. .... The School Board election, at Widnes, promises to he of a very lively character. There are fourteen candidates in the field for the eleven seats, and three distinct parties are opposing each other. Mr. !J. 11. Lee fights alone. The Nonconformists opened the campaign, on Thursday evening, by an earnest and enthusiastic meeting, and some hard knocks were given. Three very good candidates are Messrs. Snape, Brown, and Davies, and the first-named gentlernan,who has a reputation as an educationalist that reaches far beyond local circles, wid be a 'great acquisition to the Board. The party are con- I thlent of successfully carrying their candidates, and should Messrs. Timmis, Deacon, and Waring, of the Church party, be returned, and that may be taken for granted, there is little doubt that these six gentlemen would work together to carry out a progressive policy, as they are educationalists first, and denominationalists afterwards.

At one of the private. Nonconformist meetings, at which the order of the campaign was being *ranged, it was discovered that a gentleman of the Roman Catholic faith was present, and he was asked to retire. Ile Complied with the best grace he could muster.

Since performing the opening ceremony of the Runcorn Liberal Club, Mr. Brunner iI3S departed for France. Ile intends to call at Paris, where be , will new the exhibition, and combine business with pleasure in the gay captital. Afterwards he will proceed farther South. He has promised that some time in January, after his return home, he will again meet his Runcorn supporters, and he 'hopes on that occasion to be accotnanied by one of , the leaders of the party. It is reassuring to llnd that Widnes Local Board , are alive to the importance of the ferry across the nver, and having secured a comprehensive clause in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, are determined to enforce their rights. The surveyor, Mr. Iligginson. considers the accommodation proposed by the Com- pany altogether inadequate for the purpose, and anyone who peruses his report will conlially agree with him. The ferry is equally valuable to both Widnes and Runcorn, but one does not bear that the governing body of the latter town are taking any action in the matter. The protecting clause obtained by the Board of Commissioners by no means covers theground of the Widnes clause, but if their powers are limited they can at least extend their " moral simport" to the public authority of the twin town. A court for the revision of the voters' lists for the Par- liamentary division of Lmtn. was hold at the Sessions 11.415 P, on Tuesday morning. the Revising Banister being Mr. Wm. Trevor Parkins. The district prism the townships of /weft°, High Legit. Lyrnm, Thelwall, and Warburton. The Liberals were represented by Mr. A. F,. Paterson, solicitor, of altrincham, assistml by Mr. W. Skating: and the Conservatives by Mr. F. It. 11. Limisell, solicitor, of Altrineharn, assisted by Mr. C. E. ardern. —Thomas Joseph Rhoades clainted to have his name inmtrted on the register as a tenant. Fie had re. sided in New field-view situ,. January, 1889, and pnwious to that time, sinee June. 1888, he lived in a house a few yards lower down. Mr. ',indite!l held that the claim was inmmuch as the claimant's first house was not in the mme row as the one he now occupied. Mr. Rhoadelt said that Mr. Itrarstndale, the overseer, had intentionally omitted to put his name on the regMter. He had given him all the particulars, but sulsequently found that his name had not been entered. His Honour said he could not allow his claim—The Conservatives objected to the name of Edward Thomeycroft being retained on the list, as he had not occupied qualifying premises for twelve months The claimant said ire had lived in his premnt abode twelve months on the 16th of this month. His Honour said that svas not quite long enough, but on being informed that Thomeyeroft had been a house- , holder in the neighbourli.ml for ten years, allowed the vote. The Liberala objected to the name of the Gmm. mar School master, Mr. W. Ilmlop, being retained on the list. Ile was objected to on the County Council , list because he was a servant of the governors, and was ! bound to take in boarders. He was, consequently, al servant, having to leave the house when he left his I 'position as master. The vote was disallowed.

On• Monday, at the Sale Petty Sessions, a ship Canal labourer mans' Frank Mitchell was brought up in cus- tody, charged with having in his piwsession cant, eight pegs, and seven snares, at lyman on Saturday night. He was further charged with assaulting P.S. Wynne and P.O Griffiths while in the execution of their duty.— Sergeant Wynne said that at ten o'clock on Saturday night he was on duty at Statham when the prisoner and two or three other men pawil. Ile noticed that the prisoner had something bulky in kin p.A.s,sion, and he and P.C. Griffiths stopped him. They attempted to

search him, but before they could toe, he struck coot at : them right and left. They had a struggle, and the pri- soner was put on ['legroom!, when they found upon him tint. 100 yards in length. eight pegs, seven smarts, and a bag. Ile kicked like a horse when on the ground, and witness was kicked about the legs, while Griffiths hsd too hand badly injured by a kick. The magistrates fined the prisoner for having the nets in his possession £2 and costs, awl ordered the nets and pegs to be confiscated. In default of payment lie was ordered to gaol for nix weeks. For the assault on the police lw was committed for a month with hard labour.

.... John Smith, also a Ship ( anal lalanwer, was charged with having in his rweaession some nets and pegs used for the purpomof taking gain., and also with resisting PA'. Griffiths. P.C. Griffiths said that after he had assisted P.S. Wynne to lock the first prisoner up In, met , the prisoner Smith coining along Eagle-brow. tie brog- ; niSed him as one of the men in company with Mitchell, and on the way to the Hridewell prisoner tried to trip him up two or three times, and offered great resistance. Besides the net, several pegs wen, found in his pocket.— 'The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay a fine of El and costs for having Cho nets and fiegs in his rawsession, in default a month's hard labour. On the charge of re. rioting the officer, he was committed to gaol for a fur- ther term of two weeks with hard labour.

div.head: OLD WORKMEN'S CLUB.
div.p: THE OLD WORKMEN'S CLUB.

The Town-clerk of Warrington yesterday morn- ing received notice from the Charity Com- missioners, in the matter of the Charity called the Warrington Workmen's Club. to the effect that it is proposed to make an order, after the expiration of one calender month from the date of the notice, for the establishing of a scheme for the regulation of the charity in question. It is proposed to provide by the scheme that the trustees of the Charity may apply the proceeds of tile sale of the trust property towards defraying the cost of the acquisition of a site, and the erection thereon of a build- ing to be used for the purpose of a gymnasium and a reading room for the benefit of the working classes of the town—such site to be I settled upon the trustees, and the institution to be managed and conducted in accordance with rules land regulations to be approved by the Charity Com- ' miasioners. Any objections to the proposed order, or suggestions for its modification, may be sent to the Commissioners within 21 days of the date of the notice. The object named, which has, of course, received the approval of the Commissioners, is • capital one, and seems to be in accord with the original intention of the subscribers of the old Workmen's Club, as the gymnasium and reading room, if established, will be for the benefit of the working people. We are informed that many of the trustees of the old club have agreed to the pro- posal, and that Alderman Harrison has had the matter in hand.

A woman named Clarke died yesterday at Scarborough after drinking warm water in which a gross of notches had been steeped. SUICIDE iN THE THAMES. About ten o'clock on Friday morning, a man was seen to jump off the Thames Einbanknient, and before assis- I tan.- could reach him he was drowned. DISEASED REEF FOR TurrED MEAT. A Leaks butcher was on Friday rentenced to six weeks' imprisonment for having in his irkssession four stones of diseased beef, which fie stated he was about to make potted meat. THE NORTH RUCKS ELECTION. The polling in the north division of Buckinghamshire for the election of a member of Parliament cominencoi at eight o'clock on Friday morning, hut the result will not be known until to-day- (Saturday). BOILER EXPLOSION ON TILE TYNE. The holler of the steam wherry Perseverance exploded in the Tyne, at Newcastle, shortly after eight o'clock yesterday morning. The fragments were projected a considerable distance, and the wherry sank. No per- tonal injury appears to have been sustained.
